\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{まいとし} (maitoshi)}{まいとし (maitoshi)}]{\ja{まいとし} (maitoshi) — every year}

\label{lesson:JA-C75-maitoshi}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for on the way, then the Japanese for half past.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{まいとし}}
\textbf{\ja{まいとし}} — \emph{maitoshi} — \textquotedblleft{}every year\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{まいとし}} (\emph{maitoshi}) mixes the two layers: \emph{mai}, \textquotedblleft{}every\textquotedblright{}, borrowed from Chinese (Middle Chinese \emph{mwojX}), and native \emph{toshi}, \textquotedblleft{}year\textquotedblright{}, read as a kun'yomi; \emph{mainen}, with the Sino-Japanese \emph{nen}, means the same (JMdict, KANJIDIC2).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{maitoshi}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{maitoshi}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Japanese for on the way, then the Japanese for half past, then say \emph{maitoshi} again
\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{ことし} (kotoshi)}{ことし (kotoshi)}]{\ja{ことし} (kotoshi) — this year}

\label{lesson:JA-C75-kotoshi}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for half past, then the Japanese for every year.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{ことし}}
\textbf{\ja{ことし}} — \emph{kotoshi} — \textquotedblleft{}this year\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{ことし}} (\emph{kotoshi}) is a native word, usually taken apart as \emph{ko}, \textquotedblleft{}this\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{toshi}, \textquotedblleft{}year\textquotedblright{}. JMdict writes it with characters for \textquotedblleft{}now\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}year\textquotedblright{}, read as a whole for their meaning. It is inherited rather than borrowed.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{こんしゅう} (konshuu)}{こんしゅう (konshuu)}]{\ja{こんしゅう} (konshuu) — this week}

\label{lesson:JA-C75-konshuu}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for every year, then the Japanese for this year.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{こんしゅう}}
\textbf{\ja{こんしゅう}} — \emph{konshuu} — \textquotedblleft{}this week\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{こんしゅう}} (\emph{konshuu}) is Sino-Japanese (kango): two Chinese characters read with their on'yomi, readings borrowed from Chinese. They are \emph{kon}, \textquotedblleft{}now, this\textquotedblright{} (Middle Chinese \emph{kim}) and \emph{shū}, \textquotedblleft{}week\textquotedblright{} (Unihan, KANJIDIC2; Middle Chinese in Baxter's transcription).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{おととし} (ototoshi)}{おととし (ototoshi)}]{\ja{おととし} (ototoshi) — the year before last}

\label{lesson:JA-C75-ototoshi}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for this year, then the Japanese for this week.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{おととし}}
\textbf{\ja{おととし}} — \emph{ototoshi} — \textquotedblleft{}the year before last\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{おととし}} (\emph{ototoshi}) is a native word, inherited rather than borrowed, built like \emph{ototoi} with \emph{toshi}, \textquotedblleft{}year\textquotedblright{}, in place of the day. JMdict writes it with characters for \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}past\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}year\textquotedblright{}, read as a whole; its older origin is not settled.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{あさねぼう} (asanebou)}{あさねぼう (asanebou)}]{\ja{あさねぼう} (asanebou) — oversleeping}

\label{lesson:JA-C75-asanebou}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for this week, then the Japanese for the year before last.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{あさねぼう}}
\textbf{\ja{あさねぼう}} — \emph{asanebou} — \textquotedblleft{}oversleeping\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{あさねぼう}} (\emph{asanebou}) mixes the two layers: native \emph{asa}, \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{ne}, \textquotedblleft{}sleep\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{neru}, \textquotedblleft{}to sleep\textquotedblright{}, with \emph{bō}, \textquotedblleft{}monk's lodging; boy\textquotedblright{}, the on'yomi of its last character, borrowed from Chinese (Middle Chinese \emph{bjang}): a morning sleeper (JMdict, KANJIDIC2).
\end{cousinweb}
